C1.text: The actual split of chores explains only a small part of the variation in a partner's perceived fairness.
C1.reading: Supported in direction. Whole-model R² for a partner's perceived fairness is .03 to .19 in the single studies that report it (Sánchez .03, Greenstein .044, Koster .047 men and .134 women, Blair and Johnson about .15, Wilkie .19 and .11), so the split's own share is at most that. Mederer's 54% for wives is one same-source sample and its .42 for time alone is a scanned page the two readings disagree on, so check it by eye.

C2.text: Comparison referents predict a partner's perceived fairness after the actual split is accounted for.
C2.reading: Weakly and inconsistently supported. Referent effects net of the split appear for male referents in Mikula 2009 and Carriero 2016 (single studies) and are null for female referents; Hawkins's direct referent effect is lost once the wife's perceived division enters, and Grote's panel runs from inequity to comparison. The narrative reviews state the referent account as a proposal, not a tested result.

C3.text: The justifications a partner accepts for an unequal split predict that partner's perceived fairness after the actual split is accounted for.
C3.reading: Open: no study measures the justifications a partner accepts and enters them with the split. Proxies (the woman's paid hours, the husband's compensating inputs, gender ideology) predict fairness net of the split in some single studies and not in others; norm-use results in Grote & Clark 1998 sit on a page where the machine readings differ.

C4.text: A partner's perceived fairness is more strongly associated with that partner's relationship satisfaction than the actual split is.
C4.reading: Supported for women in the single studies that compare the two (Wilkie, Hu, Lavee & Katz pooled), with group exceptions in Lavee & Katz and no such pattern for men in the reviews; strength is rarely compared formally, the scales differ, and the outcome is often family-life satisfaction. The reviews' own statements that fairness is the stronger correlate are secondhand.

C5.text: The association between the actual split and relationship satisfaction is mediated by perceived fairness.
C5.reading: Suggestive, not shown. Lavee & Katz find full mediation for women and none for men, Hu a 31% partial reduction in the share coefficient, Wilkie large mediation; all are cross-sectional with no formal indirect-effect test, and Mikula's review says mediation has had little systematic study.

C6.text: Each partner over-claims their own contribution: the two partners' self-reported shares of chores sum to more than the whole.
C6.reading: Supported on average in two samples where both partners' own shares can be summed (Wilkie about 104.5%, Coundouris about 104%, group means), but Kamo's paired hours show over-claiming by husbands and not by wives, and Ross and Sicoly's direct couple test sits on a page where the machine readings differ.

C7.text: Which chores a partner does predicts that partner's perceived fairness beyond the time the chores take.
C7.reading: Indirect evidence only; no direct test. Husbands' hours in female-typed chores and the allocation of task and management work predict a wife's perceived fairness with some control for time (Blair and Johnson, Mederer, DeMaris & Longmore), but a partner's own chores beyond time is untested and Koster finds no difference between housework and child care.

C8.text: Studies measure perceived fairness of the division of chores mainly with a single self-report item.
C8.reading: Supported: 19 of the 25 studies whose own measure was quoted use a single self-report item, five of them the same NSFH item; the exceptions are multi-item scales (Mederer, Grote & Clark, Grote 2002, Kamo, Hawkins, Wilkie), and Mikula's review calls the NSFH item the base of most recent studies.

C9.text: A partner who is over-benefited by the allocation reports lower relationship satisfaction than a partner in an equitable allocation.
C9.reading: Not supported for housework. Gillespie finds no association for housework when a partner calls the allocation unfair to the partner, Wilkie's over-reward measures are null, and few partners are over-benefited (2% to 4% in Lavee & Katz); Adriaans finds lower satisfaction for the 'a bit less than my fair share' group only, and not for men.
